function.name: create_a_docker_file
function.description: This function generates a Dockerfile in the specified directory with basic configuration. The Dockerfile will be tailored to a simple Python application. Note that the provided function is in Python 3 syntax.

directory_name.description: The name of the directory where the Dockerfile will be created. It should be a valid directory path relative to the current working directory.

base_image.description: The base image to use for the Dockerfile, representing the starting point for the build.

maintainer.description: The name of the maintainer or author of the Dockerfile.

expose_port.description: The port number that the container should expose. This is typically the port that the application listens on.

entrypoint.description: The command that will be executed when the Docker container starts.

function.name: create_kubernetes_yaml_file
function.description: Generates a Kubernetes deployment and service YAML file in the specified repository directory. Note that the provided function is in Python 3 syntax.

directory_name.description: The name of the directory where the Kubernetes YAML file will be created. This should be the root directory of the repository.

deployment_name.description: The name of the deployment to be created. This should be a unique identifier for the deployment.

image_name.description: The name of the Docker image to be used in the deployment. Include the image version tag if necessary.

replicas.description: The number of replicated pods desired in the deployment.

port.description: The port number that the container exposes for communication.

service_type.description: The type of Kubernetes service to be created for the deployment.

message.content:
Below is a complete “starter kit” you can drop into the **nodejs‑welcome** repository.  
It contains:

| File | Purpose |
|------|---------|
| `Dockerfile` | Builds a lightweight Node.js image for the app |
| `k8s/deployment.yaml` | Deployment + Service for Kubernetes |
| `.github/workflows/ci.yml` | GitHub Actions workflow that builds the image, runs tests, and pushes the image to GitHub Container Registry |

> **NOTE** – The repo you mentioned (`git@github.com:zelarhq/nodejs-welcome.git`) is a Node.js project, so the Dockerfile and Kubernetes manifests are written for Node, not Python.  
> The helper functions you listed only support Python images, so we’ll hand‑craft the files instead.

---

## 1. Clone the repo

```bash
git clone git@github.com:zelarhq/nodejs-welcome.git
cd nodejs-welcome
```

> If you already have the repo locally, skip this step.

---

## 2. Create / update the files

### 2.1 Dockerfile

Create a file named `Dockerfile` at the root of the repo:

```dockerfile
# Use the official lightweight Node.js 18 image
FROM node:18-alpine

# Set the working directory inside the container
WORKDIR /usr/src/app

# Copy package.json and package-lock.json first to leverage Docker cache
COPY package*.json ./

# Install production dependencies
RUN npm ci --only=production

# Copy the rest of the application code
COPY . .

# Expose the port the app listens on
EXPOSE 3000

# Start the application
CMD ["node", "app.js"]
```

> *Why this image?*  
> `node:18-alpine` is small (~70 MB) and includes everything you need to run a Node.js app.  
> Adjust the `EXPOSE` and `CMD` lines if your app uses a different entry point or port.

---

### 2.2 Kubernetes YAML

Create a directory `k8s` (if it doesn’t exist) and add `deployment.yaml`:

```yaml
apiVersion: apps/v1
kind: Deployment
metadata:
  name: nodejs-welcome-deployment
spec:
  replicas: 2
  selector:
    matchLabels:
      app: nodejs-welcome
  template:
    metadata:
      labels:
        app: nodejs-welcome
    spec:
      containers:
      - name: nodejs-welcome
        image: ghcr.io/zelarhq/nodejs-welcome:latest   # <-- replace with your registry
        ports:
        - containerPort: 3000
        env:
        - name: NODE_ENV
          value: production
---
apiVersion: v1
kind: Service
metadata:
  name: nodejs-welcome-service
spec:
  selector:
    app: nodejs-welcome
  ports:
  - protocol: TCP
    port: 80
    targetPort: 3000
  type: ClusterIP
```

> **Image name** – If you’re using GitHub Container Registry (GHCR), the image will be pushed to `ghcr.io/<org>/<repo>:<tag>`.  
> If you prefer Docker Hub, change the image field accordingly.

---

### 2.3 GitHub Actions workflow

Create the directory `.github/workflows` (if it doesn’t exist) and add `ci.yml`:

```yaml
name: CI

on:
  push:
    branches: [ main ]

jobs:
  build:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest

    steps:
    - name: Checkout code
      uses: actions/checkout@v4

    - name: Set up Docker Buildx
      uses: docker/setup-buildx-action@v3

    - name: Log in to GitHub Container Registry
      uses: docker/login-action@v3
      with:
        registry: ghcr.io
        username: ${{ github.actor }}
        password: ${{ secrets.GITHUB_TOKEN }}

    - name: Cache node modules
      uses: actions/cache@v4
      with:
        path: ~/.npm
        key: ${{ runner.os }}-node-${{ hashFiles('**/package-lock.json') }}
        restore-keys: |
          ${{ runner.os }}-node-

    - name: Install dependencies
      run: npm ci

    - name: Run tests
      run: npm test

    - name: Build Docker image
      uses: docker/build-push-action@v5
      with:
        context: .
        file: Dockerfile
        push: true
        tags: ghcr.io/${{ github.repository_owner }}/nodejs-welcome:latest
```

> **What this does**  
> 1. Checks out the repo.  
> 2. Caches `node_modules` to speed up subsequent runs.  
> 3. Installs dependencies and runs tests (`npm test`).  
> 4. Builds the Docker image and pushes it to GHCR under the tag `latest`.

> **Prerequisites**  
> - Make sure the repository owner has permission to push to GHCR.  
> - If you’re using Docker Hub, replace the login and push steps with `docker/login-action` for Docker Hub and adjust the `tags` field.

---

## 3. Add the new files to Git

```bash
git add Dockerfile k8s/deployment.yaml .github/workflows/ci.yml
```

---

## 4. Commit & push

```bash
git commit -m "Add Dockerfile, Kubernetes manifests, and CI workflow"
git push origin main
```

> After pushing, the GitHub Actions workflow will automatically run on the `main` branch, building the image and pushing it to GHCR.

---

### Quick sanity check

1. **Build locally** (optional):

   ```bash
   docker build -t nodejs-welcome:local .
   docker run -p 3000:3000 nodejs-welcome:local
   ```

   Visit `http://localhost:3000` to confirm the app is running.

2. **Deploy to a cluster** (optional):

   ```bash
   kubectl apply -f k8s/deployment.yaml
   ```

   Verify pods are running:

   ```bash
   kubectl get pods
   ```

   Expose the service externally (e.g., via `kubectl port-forward` or a LoadBalancer) to test connectivity.

---

That’s it! You now have a fully‑functional Dockerfile, Kubernetes deployment/service, and CI pipeline ready to go. Happy coding!
